title: Synthetic data, real errors: how (not) to publish and use synthetic data
summary: Warns that conclusions drawn on synthetic data need not transfer to the real data behind it, because a single synthetic dataset hides the generative model's own uncertainty, and proposes publishing a Deep Generative Ensemble instead: several generators fitted to the same real data, so a downstream user can measure how much a finding depends on which model produced the rows. CTGAN is the generator the whole argument is instantiated on, chosen for its widespread use and for the diversity between independently trained instances, run with fixed hyperparameters across every experiment and varied in hidden-layer count for the demonstration that train-on-synthetic conclusions diverge from real ones.
affiliations: University of Cambridge; Alan Turing Institute
evidence: the experimental setup states the paper chooses a GAN architecture, specifically CTGAN, for its widespread use and its high expected diversity between individually trained models compared with VAEs, and that CTGAN is used with the same hyperparameters and architecture in all experiments; the motivating figure generates synthetic SEER prostate cancer data with CTGAN at different numbers of hidden layers and compares train-on-synthetic against train-on-real classification results

title: Differentially Private Diffusion Models Generate Useful Synthetic Images
summary: Shows that diffusion models can be trained under differential privacy to a standard where classifiers trained purely on their output are competitive on image benchmarks, using public pre-training, large batches and augmentation multiplicity to make private training tractable. The SDV paper and DP-CTGAN appear only in the bibliography, and CTGAN is cited once inside a list of differentially private GAN work; the paper is an image-domain study and runs nothing from the SDV family.
evidence: the related-work paragraph on differentially private generative models cites Xu et al. 2019 within an undifferentiated list of GAN references; the bibliography carries both the Patki et al. Synthetic Data Vault paper and Fang et al. DP-CTGAN; no SDV-family model is trained or evaluated anywhere in the paper, whose experiments are on image datasets

title: PromptEHR: Conditional Electronic Healthcare Records Generation with Prompt Learning
summary: Casts synthetic electronic health record generation as conditional language modelling: PromptEHR encodes a patient's demographics and prior visits as prompts to an encoder-decoder language model, so that longitudinal multimodal visit sequences can be generated and evaluated by perplexity rather than by tabular similarity alone. CTGAN is the tabular-generation prior art the design departs from, cited for the observation that GANs and VAEs struggle with multimodal non-Gaussian distributions and sparse one-hot vectors, and named among the conditional-GAN approaches that generate only static tabular records.
evidence: the introduction states that GANs and VAEs usually struggle to model complex multimodal and non-Gaussian distributions as well as sparse one-hot-encoded vectors, citing Xu et al. 2019; the related-work section lists conditional GANs, again citing Xu et al. 2019, among the EHR generation methods that produce only static tabular or single-modal longitudinal records, which is the limitation the language-model approach is proposed to remove

title: Data-IQ: Characterizing subgroups with heterogeneous outcomes in tabular data
summary: Separates a training set into easy, ambiguous and hard examples by tracking each example's predictive confidence and aleatoric uncertainty across training epochs, so that irreducible label noise can be told apart from model-side uncertainty and subgroups with heterogeneous outcomes surfaced. One experiment applies this to choosing between synthetic datasets: CTGAN and Gaussian Copula stand in for two synthetic data vendors, both run from the sdv-dev implementation, and the paper reports that the generator producing the higher proportion of easy examples is the one whose data trains the better real-data classifier.
affiliations: University of Oxford; Alan Turing Institute
University of Cambridge; Alan Turing Institute; University of California, Los Angeles
evidence: the appendix on principled dataset comparison states that two synthetic datasets are compared using two models representing two synthetic data vendors, namely CTGAN and Gaussian Copula, with implementations taken from github.com/sdv-dev/SDV; Table 1 ranks the CTGAN and Gaussian Copula datasets by accuracy and by proportion of easy examples across the Prostate, Covid, Support and Fetal datasets

title: Distributional Learning of Variational AutoEncoder: Application to Synthetic Data Generation
summary: Attacks the Gaussianity assumption in variational autoencoders by replacing the reconstruction term with a continuous ranked probability score, so that the decoder estimates conditional quantiles and the model learns the full distribution rather than reconstructing points, with theorems showing the objective recovers the ground-truth distribution. CTGAN and TVAE are two of the three generators DistVAE is benchmarked against across six tabular datasets, on machine-learning utility, correlation structure, marginal similarity, distance to closest record and attribute disclosure, with per-model hyperparameters and parameter counts reported.
evidence: Table 1 reports CTGAN, TVAE and CTAB-GAN against DistVAE on MARE and F1; Table 2 gives their correlation-matrix distances; later tables report their Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Wasserstein marginal similarity, distance to closest record and attribute disclosure at three neighbour counts; Table 9 lists the epochs, batch size and learning rate used for CTGAN and TVAE and Table 10 their parameter counts per dataset

title: SurvivalGAN: Generating Time-to-Event Data for Survival Analysis
summary: Identifies two failure modes specific to generating survival data, short-sightedness in the time axis and poor coverage of the censoring process, and proposes SurvivalGAN, which generates covariates first and then draws the time-to-event from a separate survival model conditioned on them, so that Kaplan-Meier curves of the synthetic data track the real ones. The tabular encoder it depends on is CTGAN's: a Gaussian mixture is fitted per continuous feature and the encoder built from it, following Xu et al. directly, and CTGAN and TVAE are also two of the five generators the result is measured against across four clinical datasets.
affiliations: University of Cambridge; Alan Turing Institute
evidence: section 4 states the paper follows the approach by Xu et al. 2019, training a Gaussian Mixture Model with NC components per continuous feature and defining the tabular encoder from it, giving training and generation over mixed continuous and categorical variables; the baselines are listed as ADS-GAN, CTGAN, TVAE, PrivBayes and NFlows; the results tables report CTGAN and TVAE on Wasserstein distance, short-sightedness, KM divergence, precision, recall and density, and the hyperparameter table records a CTGAN embedding width for the model's own encoder

title: Causality-Aware Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
summary: Attacks the feature-independence assumption in local post-hoc explanation by learning a causal graph over the data first and sampling the local neighbourhood along it, so that the perturbed instances LIME queries the black box with respect the dependencies present in the real data. SDV supplies the statistical machinery for judging that neighbourhood: the paper adopts its Gaussian mixture log-likelihood, inverted Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and its binned approximation of continuous KL divergence to compare generated instances against the real distribution, and notes that a prior method used CTGAN for the same neighbourhood-realism purpose.
evidence: the evaluation section states the paper exploits the statistical measures outlined in SDV, specifically the Gaussian Mixture Log Likelihood and the Inverted Kolmogorov-Smirnov D statistic, and describes how the SDV framework approximates continuous KL divergence by binning continuous values before computing relative entropy; the related-work section notes that another approach uses a Conditional Tabular GAN to generate more realistic synthetic data for querying the model being explained
